solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Subject that's closed, still

parts.note: a door that is pushed to is shut, so 'to' can mean closed
a still is a photograph, informally a pic

explanation.surface: A matter that has been settled yet somehow remains under discussion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'closed' gives TO in the sense of a door left to, and 'still' is a noun here, a photographic still, not an adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic is the matter under discussion, a synonym for the subject of a talk or essay.

clue.text: Go to bed — we're not joking — and rest uneasily

parts.note: to turn in is to go to bed
one's, meaning one is, is a formal impersonal way of saying we are
someone grave is serious, not joking

explanation.surface: Someone is told to go to bed in earnest, and then sleeps badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rest uneasily' is the dead being disturbed, said of someone who would be appalled by events.
explanation.definitionFit: The dead are said to rest; to be disturbed in the tomb by what the living do is to rest uneasily.

clue.text: Stuff, which you will have opened, sealed

indicators.note: the second word will have opened the first, so it sits inside it

parts.note: to stuff a cushion is to pad it
ye is an old form of you

explanation.surface: Something you have unwrapped turns out to have been firmly closed.
explanation.walkthrough: To pay is a nautical term: to waterproof a boat's seams with tar or pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: In shipbuilding, seams payed with pitch are coated to make them watertight, so sealed.

clue.text: Bottle of harmful gas found by Welshman

parts.note: CO is the formula for carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas
Jones is a very common Welsh surname

explanation.surface: A container of poisonous gas is discovered by a man from Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' looks like a container but is British slang for courage, nerve.
explanation.definitionFit: Cojones is Spanish slang for courage, the same sense as British bottle, meaning nerve.

clue.text: Part of shop makes fast returns on singular beer

indicators.note: on here means placed after the singular beer

parts.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
ale is a kind of beer

indicators.note: returns says the word for making fast is read backwards

parts.note: a boat that is made fast moors

explanation.surface: A shop part turns over quickly thanks to one beer, like a pub doing brisk trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes fast returns' reads as quick turnover, but 'makes fast' is mooring a boat and 'returns' turns it round; 'on' means after. Chambers marks the word as chiefly American.
explanation.definitionFit: A salesroom is the area of a business where goods are displayed and sold, so a part of a shop.

clue.text: Destroyer shelled navy, one's recalled

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the pieces are read in reverse
shelled means the outer letters of navy are stripped off

parts.note: one's, meaning one is, gives I and S

explanation.surface: A warship bombarded the fleet and was then summoned home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Destroyer' and 'shelled' suggest naval warfare; Siva is the Hindu god called the Destroyer.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hindu belief Siva, also spelt Shiva, is the deity known as the Destroyer within the trinity.

clue.text: Liberal president tended to be naturally sympathetic?

parts.note: Ike was the nickname of US President Eisenhower
to mind children is to tend them

explanation.surface: A liberal-minded president was inclined to be compassionate by nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tended' looks like 'was inclined' but is the minding sense, looking after.
explanation.definitionFit: People who think alike share views, and so are naturally in sympathy with each other.

clue.text: Argument to have in Cheltenham, perhaps

parts.note: a spat is a petty quarrel
to own something is to have it

explanation.surface: A row breaks out somewhere in the Gloucestershire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheltenham is an English town famous for its mineral springs; 'perhaps' says it is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheltenham grew as a resort around its mineral springs, an example of a town of that kind.

clue.text: Spaniard who painted, in place of worship, topless concubine

indicators.note: in says the painter goes inside the trimmed building
topless means the first letter, the top of this down entry's word, is removed

parts.note: a mosque is a Muslim place of worship
Salvador Dali was a Spanish painter

explanation.surface: A Spanish artist painted a semi-naked courtesan in a religious building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' fits the subject of a painting but trims M from MOSQUE.
explanation.definitionFit: An odalisque was a female slave or concubine in a harem, often painted reclining.

clue.text: Out to lunch, unexpectedly met by tearful officer's wife

parts.note: out to lunch is slang for crazy, mad

indicators.note: unexpectedly says these letters come out in an unforeseen order

explanation.surface: Someone out for a meal is surprised by the weeping wife of an officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexpectedly' rearranges MET BY TEARFUL to AMEBUTTERFLY. In Puccini's opera the heroine marries the naval lieutenant Pinkerton.
explanation.definitionFit: Puccini's tragic heroine Cio-Cio-San weds an American naval lieutenant, so she is an officer's wife.

clue.text: The city of Kyiv a jerk misspelled

indicators.note: misspelled says the letters of these words are wrongly ordered and need rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone foolish has mangled the spelling of the Ukrainian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a misspelling of Kyiv; the misspelt letters actually make another capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Reykjavik is the capital of Iceland, an example of a city.

clue.text: Fought to be heard with a gong

indicators.note: to be heard means the word is taken as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: nations that fought warred

explanation.surface: A soldier who fought in a war and earned a medal for it.
explanation.walkthrough: WARRED and WARD sound the same in standard British speech; A is placed first.
explanation.definitionFit: Gong is British slang for a medal or honour, and an award is exactly such a decoration.

clue.text: I must have both bits to eat

parts.note: the two binary digits, or bits, are one and nought, written as the letters I and O
to dine is to eat

explanation.surface: A person insists on having two pieces of food to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' looks like the speaker but is the definition: I is the chemical symbol of the element.
explanation.definitionFit: The chemical symbol for this halogen element is I, so the letter stands for it.

clue.text: Store up memoir for play

indicators.note: the letters are put in play, moved freely into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone stockpiles a memoir with a view to adapting it for the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Store up' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'Store' alone is the definition and 'up' belongs to the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An emporium is a large shop selling many kinds of goods, a synonym for a store.

clue.text: Happy to land close to snack counter!

parts.note: tiddly is British slang for slightly drunk, merry or happy
to land a prize is to win it

indicators.note: close to means the end letter of snack is taken

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted to get a job near the snack bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'counter' looks like a shop counter by the snack, but is a playing piece in the game.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiddlywink is one of the small plastic discs flicked into a cup in the game, a kind of counter.

clue.text: Crime occurring without judge hearing a thing

indicators.note: without says the letter for judge is taken away from the word for crime

parts.note: a job is criminal slang for a robbery
a court session is a hearing

explanation.surface: An offence tried in court with no judge presiding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes J from JOB, leaving OB. 'a thing' is used as in having a thing about something.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a thing about something is an idiom for a fixation, a compulsive preoccupation.

clue.text: What's up with your egg?

parts.note: a fried egg cooked on one side only is served with its yellow yolk facing upwards

explanation.surface: An enquiry about what is wrong with someone's breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's up' reads as what is wrong, but asks literally which side faces upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A fried egg served sunny side up has its bright yolk uppermost, the side that is literally up.

clue.text: Veil's collar containing a measure of brightness

indicators.note: containing says the word for collar holds the other piece inside

parts.note: to collar a suspect is to nab them
IQ, intelligence quotient, measures how bright a person is

explanation.surface: A garment's neckline features a reflective strip measured for luminosity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brightness' suggests light but means cleverness; 'collar' is a verb, to arrest.
explanation.definitionFit: A niqab is a face veil worn by some Muslim women, leaving only the eyes visible.

clue.text: Boy dispatching daughter in place of Clare

indicators.note: dispatching means sending the daughter's letter away from the boy's name

parts.note: Dennis is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A boy sends his daughter off in place of a girl called Clare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clare' looks like a woman's name but is County Clare in Ireland; Ennis is its county town.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennis is the county town of County Clare in the west of Ireland, so a place in Clare.

clue.text: Little fellow tore his pants

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the letters are made a mess of

explanation.surface: A small man ripped his trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' looks like trousers but is British slang for rubbish, signalling a rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Shortie is an informal, often teasing name for a small person, here a little man.

clue.text: Does it constitute a blanket ban on unhealthy food?

definitions.text: Does it constitute a blanket ban on unhealthy food?

parts.words: Does it constitute a blanket ban on unhealthy food?
parts.note: a blanket ban is a total ban, but blankets and sheets are both bedding, so a total ban on bad food is jokingly a sheet

explanation.surface: A question about whether a total prohibition on junk food is in force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blanket' reads as total, but bedding brings in sheets: a written list of permitted foods is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A printed list of what a dieter may eat amounts to a ban on unhealthy food, pictured as bedding.

clue.text: Cry that is about to reverberate endlessly

parts.note: sc., short for Latin scilicet, means that is or namely
re means about or concerning

indicators.note: endlessly says the word for reverberate loses its last letter

parts.note: to echo is to reverberate

explanation.surface: A shout, as it were, is about to bounce around without end.
explanation.walkthrough: SC is a less familiar abbreviation, for Latin scilicet, used like 'that is' or 'namely'.
explanation.definitionFit: A screech is a harsh, piercing shout, a kind of cry.

clue.text: Radical's irritatingly cosy life diminished

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: diminished says the phrase is cut down at both ends, leaving letters from within it

explanation.surface: A political radical's comfortable existence has been irritatingly scaled back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Radical' suggests politics but is chemistry, a group of atoms; the answer runs across the three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Glycosyl is a chemical group derived from a sugar, an example of a radical in chemistry.

clue.text: Female hit gym, then chilled

parts.note: to rap is to hit sharply
PE, physical education, is school gym

explanation.surface: A woman goes to the gym and afterwards relaxes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chilled' looks like relaxed after exercise but means iced.
explanation.definitionFit: Frappé describes a drink served iced or very cold, so chilled is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Dead weight

definitions.meaning: dead as in dead centre, meaning exactly or precisely
a lead bob hung on a line to find the vertical

explanation.surface: A heavy, lifeless load.
explanation.definitionFit: Plumb means exactly, as in plumb centre, and is also the lead weight on a builder's line.

clue.text: A lot of horses bolt

definitions.meaning: a collection of horses kept for breeding
a metal fastener, such as a rivet or boss

explanation.surface: Many horses run away.
explanation.definitionFit: A stud is a breeding establishment's group of horses, and also a fastener such as a stud bolt.

clue.text: Inclined to be having relations round last of all

indicators.note: round says the phrase for having relations goes around the other piece

parts.note: a couple who are at it are having sex

indicators.note: last of means the final letter of the word all is taken

explanation.surface: Someone is disposed to keep having affairs to the bitter end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last of all' looks like a phrase meaning finally but gives L, the last letter of 'all'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something atilt is tipped or tilted, leaning at an angle, so inclined.

clue.text: Bid at cards by fellow expert concealing nothing?

parts.note: one no trump, written 1NT, is a bridge bid; the 1 becomes I
he stands for a man or fellow
a buff is an enthusiast or expert

explanation.surface: A card player's bid is backed by a partner who knows the game and hides nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concealing nothing' reads as honest play, but means wearing nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Being naked means wearing no clothes, so nothing of the body is hidden.

clue.text: Like some Arabs, having weekend break outside the city

indicators.note: outside says the rearranged letters go round the abbreviation for the City
break says the word weekend is broken up and reassembled

parts.note: EC is the postcode district of the City of London

explanation.surface: Visitors from the Gulf enjoy a short weekend trip outside town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break' rearranges WEEKEND to EWENKED, which goes 'outside' EC. 'Arabs' are not people but Arab horses.
explanation.definitionFit: Ewe-necked describes a horse with a thin, concave neck, a fault seen in some Arab horses.

clue.text: Spouse seen in activity centre at times

parts.note: a hub is a centre of activity
by means times in multiplication, as in three by four

explanation.surface: A husband occasionally turns up at the leisure centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at times' looks like occasionally but is the multiplication sense of by.
explanation.definitionFit: Hubby is an informal word for a husband, which is a kind of spouse.
